text:
Both answers are flawed, but they differ in degree.

Assistant A gives no code, only a vague procedure. It tells the user to sort arrays that are already sorted, and its logic is wrong. Returning one array's middle element is not the median of the combined arrays. It also ignores the O(n) requirement.

Assistant B gives code, but it is also wrong in several ways:
- It raises an error when the arrays differ in length, even though the task is specifically about arrays of different sizes.
- It sorts the inputs unnecessarily, which costs O(n log n) and contradicts the O(n) requirement. It then claims the time is O(n), which is false.
- Its median calculation is wrong. Averaging arr1[mid] and arr2[mid] is not the median of the merged array, and for odd lengths it ignores arr2 entirely.

Neither answer implements the intended solution: a two-pointer merge that counts to the middle in O(n) time and O(1) space.

Assistant B is still somewhat better. It at least provides a structured implementation, correctly states the problem constraints, and would give correct results in some narrow cases. Its flaws are serious, though, including the self-contradictory complexity claim. Assistant A is shorter and equally incorrect, and it offers no usable implementation.

Overall, B is marginally more helpful because it presents actual code, even though that code does not solve the stated problem.
